findings.title: load() mutates the caller's dump entries, so reusing a dump gives wrong TTL start times
findings.property: load(arr) does not modify arr; the same dump can be loaded into several caches with the same result
findings.input: a=new LRUCache({max:5,ttl:100000}); a.set(1,'x'); d=a.dump(); new LRUCache({max:5,ttl:100000}).load(d); then inspect d[0][1].start / load d into another cache
findings.expected: d is unchanged after load (start stays the portable Date.now() timestamp), so a second load restores the intended remaining TTL
findings.actual: load assigns entry.start = perf.now() - age on the caller's entry object, replacing the portable timestamp (e.g. 1792297393352 becomes 220.9). A later load of the same array treats it as a Date.now() timestamp, computes a huge age, and the entry is immediately stale.
findings.evidence: dump() docs say its output 'can be passed to load'; load's doc says start fields 'are assumed to be calculated relative to a portable Date.now() timestamp'. After load the array violates that assumption. Mutating an input argument is also unexpected for a load/restore API.

review.title: LRUCache.load() overwrites `start` on the caller's entry objects, so reloading the same dump gives wrong TTLs
review.reason: In `src/index.ts`, `load()` runs `entry.start = this.#perf.now() - age` on the entry objects the caller passed in. That replaces the portable `Date.now()` timestamp with a `performance.now()`-relative value. `load()` documents `start` as a portable `Date.now()` timestamp and `dump()` produces exactly that format. A second `load()` of the same array therefore computes a huge age (about 1.79e12 ms), and the entry comes out immediately stale. The input is valid, the repro is deterministic, and it is not a float artefact. The fix is small, for example building a copy of the entry with the adjusted `start` before calling `#set`. The impact is narrow, because it only affects someone who reuses a dump array, so it is a low-severity but legitimate bug.
